title: Where Does Surface $χ^{(2)}$ Come From? A Systematic Derivation of Nonlinear Surface Susceptibilities from Bulk Nonlocal Response
abstract: We extend the distributional framework developed in the companion paper [Zolla, arXiv:2605.15716] to the nonlinear case, focusing on the second-order ($χ^{(2)}$) response responsible for second-harmonic generation (SHG). Starting from the most general tensorial nonlocal second-order constitutive relation and combining a spatial moment expansion with a distributional thin-layer limit, we show that the full complexity of the nonlinear interfacial response condenses, at leading order, into two scalars, the nonlinear surface susceptibilities $χ^{(2),s}_\parallel$ and $χ^{(2),s}_\perp$, associated with the tangential and normal components of the electric field, respectively. A key structural result is established: via a marginal integration over one field argument, the nonlinear surface problem reduces recursively to an effective linear one, whose surface susceptibility is determined by the bulk nonlinear kernel alone. Generalized nonlinear Maxwell boundary conditions are derived explicitly for planar and spherical interfaces, and curvature corrections are obtained systematically. The formalism is illustrated on Gaussian, Yukawa, and tensorial Lorentz kernels.
summary: This paper develops a systematic, nonlocal theory to derive nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2)}$) governing processes like Second Harmonic Generation. By combining distributional limits with moment expansions, the authors show that the complex bulk response simplifies into measurable surface coefficients. The work is significant for establishing rigorous selection rules based on material symmetry.
main_problem: The paper systematically derives nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2)}$) from the general theory of bulk nonlocal response for second-harmonic generation (SHG). It aims to quantify how interfacial effects dominate the optical response, especially when symmetry dictates zero bulk contributions.
main_result: The leading order nonlinear surface susceptibility is shown to condense into two scalar components ($\chi^{(2),s}_\parallel$ and $\chi^{(2),s}_\perp$), and the problem reduces recursively to an effective linear susceptibility determined by the bulk kernel. Furthermore, it rigorously establishes selection rules showing that centrosymmetry forbids bulk SHG.
method: The methodology combines a distributional thin-layer limit with spatial moment expansions applied to general tensorial nonlocal constitutive relations. A key technique is the 'marginal integration principle,' which simplifies the nonlinear problem into an effective linear one.
model_or_system: The study models the nonlinear optical response of material interfaces (e.g., planar or spherical) exhibiting second-order polarization ($P^{(2)}$). The theory uses general tensorial nonlocal kernels ($	ilde{\Delta}^{(n)}$) to describe interactions across space.
key_observables: Nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2),s}_\parallel, \chi^{(2),s}_\perp$), the nonlinear surface moment tensor $M^{(2,0)}_{ijk}$, and SHG amplitudes in transmitted/reflected fields.
important_parameters: The small parameter $\ell$ (thickness of the boundary layer) and the wave vector $k_0$ are crucial for analyzing the thin-layer limit. Curvature corrections appear at order $\ell^2$.
main_assumptions: Assumes rapid decay of fields, support in the bulk medium ($\Omega$), and utilizes a distributional framework extension from linear to nonlinear response.

paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first extending a linear distributional framework to the nonlinear second-order case ($\chi^{(2)}$). It then applies moment expansions in 1D and generalizes them to 3D, culminating in deriving generalized nonlinear Maxwell boundary conditions for various geometries (planar/spherical) and establishing symmetry selection rules.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework connecting fundamental material symmetries (like centrosymmetry) directly to observable optical phenomena (SHG), which is crucial for designing advanced photonic materials or understanding surface-dominated quantum interactions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic decomposition of the second-order polarization at a point r near the boundary ∂Ω. The integration domain over the two source variables (r′, r′′) splits into four cells: the homogeneous bulk contribution (top-left), a higher-order surface correction where both source points lie outside Ω(top-right), and two cross terms (bottom) where exactly one of the source points lies outside. After the distributional thin-layer limit, the two cross terms combine to produce the leading surface susceptibility χ(2),∂Ωsupported on ∂Ω.
